utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Could I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Bulatovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning to the witness. My name is Bulatovic. I am co-counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin. I will be asking you several questions. All the cautions that you were reminded of yesterday still apply. So All the cautions that you were reminded of yesterday still apply, so that we may continue our work as expeditiously as possible. You said that on the 17th of November you went to the cellar where your parents were and that your father told you that Vukovar had fallen. And that he had been told this by a police officer. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were with your father, were you there alone or were you there with perhaps another member of the ZNG from your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you spent with your parents and your father, did you perhaps talk to him about anything else in addition to the fact that Vukovar had fallen? What I have in mind specifically is, did you talk to him about what he would do? If so, please describe the conversation for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We agreed that should Vukovar fall, we would be meeting up in Zagreb; and that's all we talked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask him how he planned to escape from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him what would become of them, and he said, "Well, the same as everyone else."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he said "the same as everyone else," what precisely did he have in mind? Who was everyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The remaining civilians from the cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you had this conversation with your father, you talked for about an hour, were any of these other civilians present there? Did they have any suggestions to make? Did they say anything? If so, what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had no information from the people in the shelter, including your father, indicating how they were planning to escape from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about some weapons yesterday that you had left behind in a friend's house. I want to know: What were those weapons? You talked about a rifle. What sort of rifle? That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an M-48 and an automatic one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the calibre of this M-48 and the automatic one, respectively?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The automatic one is 7.62-millimetres, and I'm not sure about the M-48.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a PAP rifle while answering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that M-48 a PAP rifle, a semi-automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any semi-automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there were eight of you in that group, if I understood correctly what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what sort of weapons those people had.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four M-48 rifles, three semi-automatic rifles, and one automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me how much ammunition you had for each of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your weapons include hand-grenades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell me how many of those you had, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you had semi-automatic rifles, did you also have tromblons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was your flat from school, where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 50 and 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the 18th of November, 1991, how often had you gone back to your flat, I mean from the time that you joined the ZNG on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice a week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The cellar in which your parents were staying, is that the same cellar that belongs to your building in which your flat was, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the reason was for you going back to your flat twice if your parents were there, and perhaps they could see if everything was all right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there to see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think my question was clear: How many times did you go back to your flat. As far as I understand your parents were in the cellar. If your parents were in the cellar, why would you need to go back to your flat since they were there to do it for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody went back to the flats just to check if everything was all right. Everybody was in the cellars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a TV set, a radio in your flat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the school where your unit was positioned, what about there, did you have a TV set or a radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time during your time and involvement with the ZNG have an opportunity to watch TV or follow the radio programme?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for as long as there was electricity. When there was a power cut, we were no longer able to follow anything at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you specify the time-line. Until which point in time was it possible to watch TV, and when it start to be impossible? When was the power cut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the moment when you dropped your weapons and you headed for the hospital with that friend. In your statement to the OTP you stated his full name. Given the protective measures that are in place, I will avoid mentioning this person's name, but I will ask you a different thing. This person, your neighbour, was he with you throughout? And I mean from the moment in time you left the weapons behind in the neighbour's house to the your departure for Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken to Mitrovica together also?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you released from Mitrovica together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet while in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the details of your arrest on the 18th [as interpreted] of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction, please. Page 6, line 2 it says "the 18th," and I said "the 19th," the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we consider the 19th to be the day of your arrest, because you said you were arrested on that date, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were stopped by a vehicle with four soldiers in it. Can you first of all please explain what sort of a vehicle was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a green Jeep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were four soldiers in this vehicle; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the Jeep disgorged a person that you were later to recognise. I will ask you about that later on. You recognised that person as Veselin Sljivancanin. Can you please describe the Veselin Sljivancanin that you saw. Uniform, weapons, the whole works, everything about the way you perceived or saw that person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Jeep pulled over, the door opened and this gentleman asked us where we were headed. My neighbour and I said, We are going to the hospital. He told us to get on and that he would drive us there. Once we reached the hospital and got off the Jeep, the gentleman told the soldiers manning the gate --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but that wasn't my question. I asked you to describe this man that you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a camouflage uniform. He was tall and sported a moustache, and he had a Tito cap with a red star on his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any weapons; and if so, what sort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw no weapons on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was his rank displayed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this same man in that photograph that you saw in the newspapers, the one you told us about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this same person on TV, too, the person fitting that description?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I was released from the camp, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of your activities and involvement with the ZNG, as far as I understand, based on your answers today you were relatively well-armed. Can you please describe your combat operations your combat activities. How did you carry those out? Where? What were the groups? Who devised the plans? Who was in command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't do anything where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I understand, throughout the war, throughout the armed conflict in Vukovar, you did not fire a single bullet, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The APCs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were firing at military APCs, that is some sort of armed operation or armed action. What I want to know is how this came about. Why did you start firing? Who was in command? Who gave you orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody gave us orders. When the APCs set out, they were the first to start firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't be asking you any further questions about that; this is crystal clear. There is something else, though, that I want to know about. You arrived with the soldiers on the 19th. They met you in the street. They gave you a ride in this Jeep all the way to the hospital. How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You conducted a conversation with soldiers there, that is based on your statement to the OTP, and you found out that these soldiers were from Cacak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers offered you cigarettes, didn't they? You said so yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take it - I think you'll probably agree - that your conversation, your neighbour's conversation, with those soldiers was friendly to a fault, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should ask my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were there, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you witnessed the conversation, but all right. In a way I understand your hostility. Let me ask you something else. Did the army ask for any information from you? They gave you cigarettes, they talked to you, so how did you reach the point where you started discussing weapons? Was that topic first started by your friend or by you or by them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers asked us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they ask you, and who in fact asked you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who put us on the APC to take us to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they ask you, and how did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked us whether we had had any weapons. The neighbour said we did. They asked: Where? And then we told them where. And then we went to that location and surrendered our weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the army people tell you after you had surrendered your weapons? Did they ask you where you were from, what were you doing in your locations, where were your positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't ask us anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they beat you there when you surrendered your weapons, when you took them to the spot where you had left your weapons? Did they mistreat you in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell me what time it was on the 19th of November 1991 when you were brought to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 6.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to repeat my question because I think there is a problem with the transcript. The answer and the question got all mixed up, so I will repeat my question to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was it when you were brought to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they take you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Velepromet, how many other civilians were there in the yard of Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific. What is a lot, in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I had to have my hands on my back and put my head down, so I wasn't able to look around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm only interested in what you were able to see. So please tell us, given what you were able to see, how many civilians were there there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said just a minute ago that there were a lot of them, so you were able to see that there were a lot of people. I'm interested in defining what "a lot" means for you. Is it over 100? Over 1.000? Can you give us some kind of a reference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, I wasn't able to look around, so I could only see what I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's precisely what I am interested in. What were you able to see? How many people were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean you don't know the exact number? Is that what you're saying? I'm not interested in the exact number; I'm just interested in defining a bit closer what "a lot" means.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you something? You said that you had weapons and ammunition. How much ammunition did you have to go with your rifles, a lot or a little?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever we were able to carry, that's all we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how much was that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your answer. The interpreters did not understand what you said when I asked you how much ammunition did you have.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 500 bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These 500 bullets, where did you keep them? Was it in your combat set or was it in a some kind of a clip that you carried? What was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no clips.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you were all issued with 500 bullets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, how many bullets did you have, each of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever we were able to carry with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I keep asking you: How much were you able to carry with you and what did it depend on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I had I surrendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how much you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 500 bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us turn back to Velepromet. You said that first you stayed in one room and were later moved to another room. Is that right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the distance between the two rooms and also where these two rooms were positioned, the first one and then the second one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we left the first room we entered the second room. It was maybe 5, 10, or 15 metres away, in the same building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the size of the second room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: In the same that you gave to the OTP investigators in 1995, in relation to the time when you were transported from the hospital to Velepromet, you said that Mr. Sljivancanin had told you that he would transfer you in his van to the hospital. Today you mentioned no van whatsoever. Would you please tell us: What was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the OTP, you said that Mr. Sljivancanin -- this is how you identified him, as the man who asked you where you were going. You said that he told you that he would transport you to the hospital in a van. Today you told us that the soldiers who stopped you were in a Jeep, a Jeep and a van are two very different things. Could you please explain this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were transported to the hospital in a Jeep. Later on they took us to Velepromet in an APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us here that you were questioned, as I understood yesterday, by the representatives of the Serb Territorial Defence. And you said that there were 20 other people listening to you there. I would like to learn more about the method of this questioning. Were you questioned one by one, one after the other? Did you sign -- did you write some statements there? Did you sign perhaps any typed statements? I'm just interested in learning more about this procedure which took place in Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 20 of us who went out and went to this other room. The gentleman who introduced himself as a military policeman, upon recognising me, took me aside. He asked me about the types of weapons I had, how many Serb children I had killed, how many necklaces I had made out of fingers and ears. We didn't write any statements and we didn't sign anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this taking place in the room where all of you were, or did this man take you outside, where you were able to talk alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us were in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As this man was taking to you, the others were listening. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the man questioning you recognised you. How was he able to recognise you? Was he a local resident of Vukovar, or how did he know you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a resident of Vukovar, and we knew each other from fishing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 19th in Velepromet, do you remember how many buses you saw there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, you spoke about how there were initially 60 of you and then 38 remained. Can you give us the names of some people you remember out of those 38 who were with you. If you think that it could in any way reveal your identity, then we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Vuletic; Emil Cakalic; Djoko Vladisavljevic, Djordje. I can't remember the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From that moment on after this questioning in Velepromet and until the information you questioning you had in February in Sremska Mitrovica in 1992, did anybody else talk to you in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote a statement on the 20th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I misspoke. I said "February" and I meant January. So from the 19th of November, 1991, until late January 1992, did anybody else speak to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody spoke to me until the 20th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that in Sremska Mitrovica you received no information, no newspapers, no TV, no radio. So it was an information blackout. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP, you talk about the way in which you recognised Veselin Sljivancanin. You say that you saw his photograph in some military magazine. In the context of what you have just told us, the fact that you had no printed media there to use or to read, how on earth does this magazine suddenly appear, just out of the blue, in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't get anything until the Geneva Conventions arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the International Red Cross arrived, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days before your release was that, before you were allowed to go back to Croatia before you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: December, the 12th [as interpreted] of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember about December 1991? Did you speak to any representatives of the International Red Cross in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe there is something on page 15, line 11. It says "December, the 12th of December." I don't think the witness was speaking about the 12th of December. I think he was speaking about the 12th month of the year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except for your contact with the International Red Cross in Sremska Mitrovica in December 1991, was there any other time that you were contacted by them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the inmates had contacts with them, but no personal contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "all the inmates," what do you mean? What sort of contact did they have? I did not mean a personal acquaintance. I meant were you in contact officially?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to our room. They brought us books, magazines, and asked if there was anything else we needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to this conversation, no other conversation ever took place, did it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent messages to our families in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we go back into private session briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the names of certain people. Please tell me if they ring a bell. If so, what do you know about those people. The first name is Ivo Madzarevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Branko Krizmanic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Filip Karaula?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Marin Pliso?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ivica Arbanas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ante Roso?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you about your return from Sremska Mitrovica. Following your return from Sremska Mitrovica, did you have any further contacts with the International Red Cross, first of all in Mitrovica immediately before your release or later, following your release, or when you arrived in Zagreb or wherever else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Mitrovica when we were about to be exchanged. In Zagreb I had no further contacts with these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At your exchange when you had these contacts with them, did you have to fill in a form, an exchange form, an official document that they gave you, to record some information for their sake? How long you spent in detention, where and when you were arrested, what the conditions were in detention, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you never filled in any sort of form or questionnaire, none of the International Red Cross people ever took any statements from you concerning the time you spent in detention, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just wrote messages, but I can't remember that we ever wrote anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any rights that you acquired on the strength of the fact that you had been detained in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you entitled to any sort of compensation or any special rights or privileges just because you had been detained in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we ask that the document in full be put in in due course because this would only seem to be these two pages, apart of the list of people detained at Sremska Mitrovica prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there a relevance the in the case of the full document?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Well, it may also contain evidence of people who gave evidence here, that they were also detained in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it a document that is in full in the electronic record?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: That I'll have to find out for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, when you found out you can raise it again. At the moment we'll receive into evidence these two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will be exhibit 133 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I told you that official documents of the Government of Croatia indicate that you were arrested on the 18th of November, 1991, and that both of your brothers were arrested on the same day and that on the 20th of November your friend and neighbour was arrested, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What do you mean, arrested on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were arrested on the 19th, and I'm telling you that the official documents of the Government of Croatia indicate that it wasn't on the 19th but rather on the 18th, which means that on the 19th you were not in the hospital, as you have told us here. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in the hospital on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Yes, Mr. Agha. Re-examined by Mr. Agha:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you're ready I have a number of questions which I'd like to clarify -- for you to clarify which the learned Defence counsel have asked you. Now, during your cross-examination you were asked during your guard duty at the building what it meant in practical terms, and you side that you were to see whether any APCs or military people were starting to arrive from the direction of the barracks. You also said later that the barracks was not under siege. So what was going on in the barracks during this period of time, if you were able to keep an eye on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unable to see because the barracks is at an elevation, on a hill, and it is I don't know how far from my building. However, the commander had told us if I saw them coming down I should inform him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort did the barracks, if you're aware, play in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, turning to another area of the questions which the learned Defence counsel asked you, you were asked during cross-examination which particular ZNG unit was stationed at the palace of Count Eltz and you said you did not know. Do you know if any ZNG unit at all was based in the palace of Count Eltz in the months of July and August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, recently, this morning, in cross-examination the learned Defence counsel asked you about when you went to visit your parents, and you said that you were able to watch TV and radio at their house. What did you hear on the radio or TV about the hospital, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I have to intervene finally. I didn't manage to intervene when the question pertained to the barracks. This witness said that he went to the basement; he didn't go to the apartment to watch television or anything like that. He didn't say this, and I believe this question is extremely leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think leading is the issue, Mr. Borovic, because he's trying to remind the witness of evidence. But your reminder, it seems to me have misunderstood the evidence. I don't think what you said there was the evidence at all, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, and I will have to check the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, before you go through your understanding, what we're more interested in is the witness's. It might be better if neither of us discussed what we think the evidence was but you learn from the witness what his understanding of the truth is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in cross-examination were you asked this morning whether you went to your parents' house to -- and were able to see the TV and listen to the radio?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cross-examined this witness, and I did not put such a question to the witness. You can verify this in transcript. All I did is ask the witness whether he went to his apartment and whether he had a TV and a radio sets in his apartment. I didn't ask him whether he watched or listened to TV or radio in his apartment. I only asked him whether there was a TV set or a radio set at the school and whether they watched and listened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That roughly accords with my recollection, Mr. Bulatovic. Now we've exposed it all. I suggest, Mr. Agha, if you want to follow it up, you might ask the witness where it was, if in any place, that he watched TV or heard radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for clarification, Witness, did you have the opportunity at all to hear the TV or radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen to the radio, yes, but watch TV, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you hear anything on the radio about the hospital? Was there any discussion about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard from Dr. Bosanac that the hospital had been shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear anything on the radio regarding the JNA barracks, what it was up to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you leave it, the Chamber would be interested to know where he heard the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please clarify for the Chamber where you heard the radio.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the basement where my parents were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I now may turn to a different area, and I'll try to start with this morning's cross-examination. Now, this morning the Defence counsel, learned Defence counsel, mentioned that when a green Jeep reached the hospital gates - and you were asked about that, and you said that a gentleman got out and told the soldiers manning the gates - at that point you were cut off. What did the gentleman tell the soldiers who were manning the gates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told them to watch us and that he would send a vehicle to transport us to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that gentleman who said he would send the vehicle to Velepromet for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, staying on the subject of Mr. Sljivancanin, during cross-examination you indicated that you were able to recognise him from a picture and that there was a blackout in Sremska Mitrovica until 12th December, 1991, when the Red Cross arrived. When, roughly, were you able to see that picture in which you recognised Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we indicate that our recollection is that the 12th was mentioned, but there was some confusion over the translation. We understand it was the 12th month rather than the 12th day. So there may be a misunderstanding in what you're putting to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just to clarify, when, roughly, did you see the picture of Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a few days before the Geneva Conventions arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving to another area during your cross-examination, and that was this morning again, you were asked about the state of your arms and it was suggested that you indicated that you were relatively well-armed. What heavy weaponry did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the positions where we were, we had no heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move to your evidence regarding Velepromet. Now, during cross-examination you indicated that you arrived at Velepromet at 6.30 a.m. on the 19th of November. You said that you saw a lot of civilians in the yard, although you could not name the exact number. Why were you not kept in the yard with the other civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived at the gate of Velepromet, we were told to put our hands on our backs and bend our heads down. We entered the yard. As soon as we came out, some of the soldiers said: Here are the MUP men. I don't know how come I wasn't with civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you were not kept in the yard, where did they take the MUP men and you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just me and my neighbour. They took us to the room that we called the death room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during your entire cross-examination, both yesterday and today, the learned Defence counsel have raised various questions regarding Velepromet. For example, the exit, the entry, the yard, the rooms. Now, do you remember Velepromet? Would you be able to recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence did not object to the previous question, but we believe that this question is leading. The witness yesterday talked about the room where he was kept and where the room was. And this question suggests how the witness should answer. The witness clearly indicated yesterday that he remembered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the question of what recollection the witness has of Velepromet, I believe, properly arises for re-examination based on a variety of questioning from more than one Defence counsel. He gave descriptions in varying degrees, first of arrival at Velepromet, and then of where he was held, where he was moved to, where he was questioned. And I think those, put together, properly give rise to the question: How much do you remember about Velepromet, tell us? This question is putting that to him; it's not in any way, as I see it, telling him how to answer. It's asking him: You tell us what, if anything, you remember. So I think it's a fair question. Yes, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you kindly tell the Chamber of your recollections of Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember our arrival, the way we were searched and taken to that room and then to a different room. Then we were taken back and we left for the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, again I want to stay with Velepromet, and the questions now I am going to ask you relate to the questions which learned Defence counsel asked you yesterday which concerned the statement which you gave to the OTP in 1995. Now, yesterday during cross-examination you looked at your statement and you saw that you had not referred to the room where you were kept as a room of death. You explained that you had nicknamed the room where you were staying as a room of death. In 1995, when you gave your statement, did the investigators ask you whether you had given the room where you were staying a particular nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again turning to your statement, I would like to clarify an issue which is based on that statement which you gave in 1995. Now, you mentioned in that statement that you were maltreated or abused at Velepromet. Now, there seems to be some confusion, based on the cross-examination, whether you were maltreated at all at Velepromet or whether the maltreatment related to whether it was just in the room where you were not maltreated. So could you perhaps, with the assistance of the Chamber, refer to the statement and we can actually see what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And if I may kindly ask the court usher to provide the witness with his statement in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any particular page or paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement yesterday you were asked to read a part of your statement which started: "There were between 50 and 60 of would you say in that room."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: That's on page 3 and it's in the bottom part, at least in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the witness is turning to page 3. It would help him a lot if he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you could kindly turn to page 3 of your statement and find the part where it says: "There were all together 50 or 60 people in that room." Would you kindly read that part from there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "There were all together 50 or 60 people in that room. I was not maltreated, but I saw a man."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you stop there, please, Witness. Now, when you say you were "not maltreated," that refers to, as I understand, you not being maltreated whilst you were in that room. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This must be a leading question. I think the right way to ask would be: What does this mean? And not to suggest a possible meaning to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're quite right, Mr. Vasic. I'm afraid the harm's been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I apologise to the Chamber and to my learned friends. If the witness could kindly answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not maltreated for as long as we were there, but when we came back, my hands were tied by a length of wire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if I can ask you to go to the final page of your statement which relates to the portion in which you were outside of the room of death. Could you please read, and I'll tell you when to stop, on the English roughly about four lines from the bottom. And it starts: "This interrogation lasted about 10 minutes." It starts: "This interrogation lasted about 10 minutes. I was sitting in that room and I was not -- I was approached by a man. His nickname was Topola," that part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no objection to the witness reading out the relevant portion, but I think it would be proper to read the previous sentence because that previous sentence is important in the general framework of what the witness is testifying about and what the witness testified about his interrogation. And my learned friend seems to have forgotten about that first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I have no objection to that first sentence being read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber hasn't seen the statement, so we are in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I have no objection whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So perhaps if you could read from the top, almost, of the statement: "He wanted to handcuff me, but he could not find handcuffs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you find that passage in the statement: "He wanted to handcuff me but he couldn't find handcuffs"? Can you find that there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I perhaps give you a hand with this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Vasic, but he's found it now. Yes. Would you be able to read that aloud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "He wanted to handcuff he, but he could not find any handcuffs. And he tied my hands with a length of wire. He did not beat me during the interrogation. The interrogation lasted about 10 minutes. I was sitting in that room when I was approached by a man by the name of Topola from Negoslavci. (I cannot remember anything else about him; that was the first time I saw him.) He gave me a bullet for the pistol and he ordered me to swallow the bullet. Under the circumstances, I had no choice but to do it. He left, but he later returned and gave me another bullet to swallow. He taunted me by saying that I was an Ustasha and made me swallow the other bullet. He hit me several times over the head, but he did not injure me. This was psychological torture. After that, we returned to the room."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, that's sufficient. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And do you want the witness to indicate whether that is his recollection or not today?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness, is that your recollection of the events today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Agha, we're almost at the end of the tape. Will you be long?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I think possibly about 10 more minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In that case, we'll have to have the break now, I think. Yes. We will resume at 10 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just before I continue to complete my re-examination, the last exhibit by the learned Defence counsel was Exhibit 133, which dealt with two pages of the entire list. And it was suggested that if I could search the electronic copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I have done this now and I understood a copy had been provided to the learned Defence counsel in entirety under Rule 68. So for a matter of completeness I wonder if it could be helpful to the Chamber and to future witnesses if the document could actually be exhibited in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will tender that in your re-examination, Mr. Agha. It will be received in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not yet in the electronic record it seems, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Not as yet, unfortunately, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ah, well, you will have to wait or somebody else will have to deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: The joys of E-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, let us hope that by the 23rd of January we can actually mean "the joys of E-court." We'll hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, just before we broke for the recess we were looking at your statement which you gave, based on which numerous questions were asked you by the learned Defence counsel. Now, during your cross-examination you were asked about the policeman who was taken out of the room of death, and there seems to be some confusion, I would submit, about what you said in your statement about the manner in which that policeman died. So -- or indeed what happened to him. So if you could please return to the bottom of page 3 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid the witness never said he saw the police officer die. He talked about indications and sounds, but he never for a moment claimed that he saw the police officer dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As usual, you're spot on, Mr. Vasic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And this is the point, Your Honour, I'd like to clarify to what he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You see the problem with the way you've introduced it?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Agha, you're not the only counsel present here who doesn't. I can look to the other side and identify people, but it does happen and it's happening a bit too often for everybody's comfort that the people are jumping to presumptions about the evidence and putting them to witnesses when it is not the evidence. So I would hope all counsel try and discipline themselves about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, could you turn to page 3 of your statement and read from the part which is towards the bottom of the statement, and it starts with: "Later, I cannot remember when, he was taken away from the room."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Later, I cannot remember when, he was again taken away from the room by JNA soldiers. We heard him scream with pain. After that, he never came back to our room. I did not see them kill him, but on the way out of our room when we were being taken to the JNA barracks, I saw traces of blood on the floor and his body was lying in a room that looked like a toilet."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, is that your recollection today of what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, turning to another part of your statement, during cross-examination by the learned Defence counsel you were asked why you had not mentioned the statement which you gave in Sremska Mitrovica prison to the OTP in 1995, when you were interviewed. Now, can you please go to the final three lines of your statement and just read those, please, for the benefit of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "JNA soldiers woke us up at about 8 a.m. and made lists of names, giving us each two packs of cigarettes and some food" --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, Witness, if you could skip to the final three lines, that would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I spent four and a half months in Sremska Mitrovica and was eventually exchanged on the 27th of March, 1992. If necessary, I can provide a statement concerning my time in the camp. This is everything I can say about the events that I have been asked to describe. End of statement."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, later on did the OTP request you to give another statement regarding your time in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave no other statements but this one -- or rather, I don't remember. Perhaps I did, perhaps I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd actually like now to turn to that statement which you gave in Sremska Mitrovica prison camp, and you told the Court that your statement was untruthful because if you told them everything they would have abused you more severely. Now, this relates to the statement you gave in Sremska Mitrovica prison. Now, when in 1995 you gave your statement to the OTP, what kind of the abuse did the ICTY investigators subject or threaten you to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat that question for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gave your statement in 1995 to the Office of the Prosecution, what kind of threats and abuse did the Office of the Prosecution subject you to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no abuse whatsoever, but I didn't write anything else in addition to this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this statement which you gave to the OTP in 1995 truthful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what respects is it not truthful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing about it was truthful; it was all lies and untruths.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm referring to the 1995 statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor. Was that truthful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said back in 1995 is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And this completes my re-examination. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Agha. I believe the next witness is a protected witness. Is that correct? Yes. The screens could be run down now while I'm speaking. Thank you very much. You'll be pleased to know that that concludes your questioning. The Tribunal is very grateful to you for the assistance that you have given us and for your coming here to The Hague to assist in this case. You'll be pleased to know that you may, of course, now return to your home and whatever else you want to do. So thank you; you may go out now with the court officer. Mr. Agha, just one matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a very solemn matter. The Chamber has had it drawn to its attention that we will not see you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I'm afraid that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May we wish you well in your knew career in Sierra Leone and we hope you find life personally and professionally satisfying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I would like to thank the Chamber for its kind observations and also the learned Defence counsel for the work we have done together as well as the court officers and the translators. Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Your Honour, there is one matter -- indeed two matters that I would like to clarify. Could they be done in closed session, if that's possible, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: They relate to this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you mean fully closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's the shutters which is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, the shutters are unimportant in relation to these points, but as long as the matters I am going to be mentioning are not heard outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session will achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. For reasons which have been discussed in private session, the most practical course the Chamber is persuaded at this point is not to commence the evidence of the witness who has just been sworn. There is no prospect of completing that witness's evidence in the time available, and because of his health it would be unfair to adjourn partway through his evidence. So the most practical course, unfortunately, is now to adjourn. And hopefully the witness will be well enough to attend when we resume sitting at the commencement of the new year. So for those reasons and in those circumstances, we now adjourn to the new year. May we wish everybody a very appropriate break and seasonal greetings. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd day of January, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.40 a.m.,
